title: Designing a Clickstream Analytics Pipeline, End to End
hook: Every click becomes a dashboard number. Here are the 6 design steps in between.
hook_options: Every click on a website becomes a row in a dashboard. Here's every step in between.
Design a clickstream pipeline: the system design question, answered step by step.
From one click event to a gold table: Kafka, streaming, watermarks and partitions.

sources.claim: Topics are partitioned across brokers; same key goes to same partition; consumers read a topic-partition in written order (ordering is per partition)
Each partition is consumed by exactly one consumer within a subscribing consumer group; consumer position is one offset per partition
Kafka idempotent producer: broker dedupes resends using producer ID and sequence number
Event time is the time embedded in the data; Structured Streaming end-to-end exactly-once needs replayable sources (offsets, checkpoints) and idempotent sinks
Watermark = max event time seen minus late threshold; data under the threshold is never dropped (strict), later data best effort; dropDuplicates with watermark
Bronze = raw unvalidated data; silver = cleaned, validated, deduplicated; gold = aggregated data for analytics and reporting
BigQuery partition pruning: a qualifying filter on the partitioning column scans matching partitions and skips the rest, reducing bytes processed
DuckDB pushes filters on Hive partition keys down into files (pruning)
DuckDB INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING/DO UPDATE requires UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY constraint

scenes.beat: Title line lands in the first second; a single click dot travels left to right through six labelled boxes and ends as a number on a dashboard tile.
on_screen_text: Every click becomes a dashboard number
scenes.narration: Every click on a website becomes a number on a dashboard. Between the click and the number are six design decisions worth knowing cold: Kafka partitions, batch versus streaming, late data and watermarks, idempotent writes, bronze, silver and gold, and partition pruning. We'll build the whole pipeline on one nine-row table, and every query you see was actually run.

scenes.beat: A page view, a click and a purchase each drop out of a browser icon as a row card; the two timestamp fields highlight one after the other.
on_screen_text: Clickstream: one row per user action
scenes.narration: A clickstream is the log of what users do: page views, clicks, purchases. Each action becomes one event. We treat events as append-only: a click that happened, happened. So every action is a new row. Two timestamps matter. event_time is when the action happened. ingest_time is when our pipeline received it. Keep those two apart, because half of this video depends on the gap between them.

scenes.beat: DataTable of all 9 rows in arrival order; the second copy of event 3 flashes, then event 6 slides to the bottom with its arrival time highlighted.
scenes.narration: Here's the table we'll use for the whole video, in the order rows arrived. Three users: 101, 102 and 103. Most events land about a second after they happen. Two rows are trouble. Event 3, a click by user 102, shows up twice, the second copy 44 seconds after the first, like a retry. And event 6, a purchase by user 101, happened at 09:04 but only arrived at 09:21:40. Nine rows, but only eight real events. Every chapter fixes one problem in this table.

scenes.beat: Hook card; the word 'topic' is struck through and replaced by 'partition'.
scenes.narration: Kafka does not keep your whole topic in order. It keeps each partition in order. That one sentence answers a lot of Kafka interview questions.

scenes.beat: PartitionGrid: a 'clicks' topic splits into three partition lanes on three broker boxes; events drop into lanes and stay in sequence inside each lane.
on_screen_text: Topic: a named stream of events
One partition: read in the order written
scenes.narration: Our click events land in a Kafka topic, say one called clicks. A topic is split into partitions, and those partitions are spread across the brokers in the cluster. Inside one partition, a consumer reads events in exactly the order they were written. Across partitions there's no such promise. An event in partition zero and an event in partition two have no defined order relative to each other.

scenes.beat: Events colour-coded by user_id route into lanes; all of user 101's events stack in one lane in sequence: page_view, click, purchase.
on_screen_text: User 101: view, click, purchase in order
scenes.narration: So how do you get the order you actually need? With the key. Events with the same key go to the same partition. If we key by user_id, every event from user 101 lands in the same partition, and a consumer reads page view, then click, then purchase, in the order they were written. Different users can sit on different partitions, and that's fine, because 'what did this user do next' is a per-user question.

props.afterLabel: Key = user_id: same user, same partition

scenes.beat: Three consumer boxes in one group each attach to one partition lane; an offset pointer ticks forward on each lane.
on_screen_text: Consumer group: consumers sharing a topic
Each partition: one consumer in the group
scenes.narration: Now reading. Consumers subscribe as a consumer group. Within the group, each partition is consumed by exactly one consumer. That's how Kafka splits the work, and it's why per-partition order survives: one partition, one reader in the group. The group's position is small: one offset per partition, which marks how far it has read. Remember that offset. It's what makes replay possible in chapter four.

scenes.beat: Comparison: left 'whole topic ordered' with a red cross, right 'ordered per partition, keyed by user_id' with a tick.
on_screen_text: Q: How do you keep a user's events in order?
Order is per partition, not per topic
scenes.narration: Interview version. 'How do you guarantee a user's events are processed in order?' Key the events by user_id. Same key, same partition. Ordering is per partition, not per topic, and one consumer in the group reads each partition.

props.verdict: Order is per partition, not per topic

scenes.beat: Callout takeaway card.
on_screen_text: Takeaway: order lives in the partition
Pick the key that matches your question
scenes.narration: Takeaway: order lives in the partition, so pick the key that matches the question you need answered in order.

props.label: Takeaway
props.detail: Pick the key that matches your question

scenes.beat: Hook card with two clocks: 'event_time' and 'ingest_time'.
on_screen_text: First decide which clock you trust.
scenes.narration: Batch or streaming? Before you pick, decide which clock your numbers follow.

props.title: Batch or streaming?
props.subtitle: First decide which clock you trust.

scenes.beat: Comparison: left a bucket of rows processed once and closed; right a conveyor of rows processed continuously.
on_screen_text: Batch: process what has landed, then stop
Streaming: keep processing as events arrive
scenes.narration: Batch means: take the events that have already landed, say all of yesterday, process them, and finish. Streaming means the job keeps running and processes events as they arrive. Same events, same business logic. The difference is when the work runs, and how much of the data has shown up when it runs.

scenes.beat: DataTable with event_at, arrived_at and lag columns; the lag column fills in row by row and event 6's 0:17:40 is highlighted.
on_screen_text: Event time: the time inside the data
Ingest time: when it reached us
scenes.narration: This is where the clocks matter. Spark's docs define event time as the time embedded in the data itself, not the time it arrived. Look at the lag column. Most events arrive a second after they happen. Event 6, a purchase, took seventeen minutes and forty seconds. A batch job that runs after it has landed simply sees it. A streaming job counting purchases per minute has to decide what to do when a 09:04 purchase shows up at 09:21.

scenes.beat: FlowGraph: Kafka offsets feed a checkpoint box; the job box crashes, restarts, and resumes from the checkpoint marker.
on_screen_text: Spark tracks how far each stream has read
Restart: pick up from the checkpoint
scenes.narration: A streaming job also has to survive restarts. Spark Structured Streaming tracks how far it has read with source offsets and checkpoints, so after a failure the source can be replayed from where the job was. Hold on to that. It's half of exactly-once in chapter four.

scenes.beat: Callout: a question bubble 'freshness?' points to two cards, batch and streaming; both cards share a footer 'GROUP BY event_time'.
on_screen_text: Ask first: how fresh must the numbers be?
Let the requirement pick the mode
scenes.narration: In an interview, don't declare a winner. Ask how fresh the numbers need to be, and let that requirement pick the mode. We won't quote cost or latency figures here, because those depend on your system. What doesn't depend on your system: if you bucket by arrival time instead of event time, a late purchase lands in the wrong minute.

props.text: Ask first: how fresh must the numbers be?
props.label: Interview tip
props.detail: Let the requirement pick the mode. Either way, bucket by event_time.

scenes.beat: Callout takeaway card.
on_screen_text: Takeaway: ask how fresh it needs to be
scenes.narration: Takeaway: ask how fresh the numbers need to be, and let that pick the mode. Event time picks the bucket.

props.text: Ask how fresh it needs to be
props.label: Takeaway

scenes.beat: Hook card; a late row approaches a dashed watermark line and pauses.
scenes.narration: Late data is not automatically dropped. A watermark decides, and it doesn't use the wall clock.

scenes.beat: Timeline: a 09:00-09:10 window box stays open while dots keep trickling in from the right.
on_screen_text: A straggler could always show up
Threshold: how late can data be?
scenes.narration: Say you count purchases per ten-minute window. When is the 09:00 window finished? A straggler could always show up. A job that never ends can't wait forever, so Spark asks you for a threshold: how late can data be and still be counted?

events.label: A straggler could still show up
Threshold: how late can data be?

scenes.beat: Timeline: a 'max event time' marker moves right; a watermark line trails it by the threshold; rows left of the line turn amber, not red.
on_screen_text: watermark = max event time seen - threshold
Later than that: best effort, may drop
scenes.narration: Here's the rule from the Spark docs. The watermark is the maximum event time the engine has seen, minus your threshold. Data that is less late than the threshold is guaranteed to be processed. Data later than that may be dropped, or may still be counted. Spark only promises best effort there. So never say 'late data is dropped'. Say 'data beyond the watermark isn't guaranteed'.

events.label: Later than that
events.detail: best effort: may drop, may count

scenes.beat: CodePanel with the query; DataTable fills in arrival order; event 6's 'behind' cell pulses, then its t_10min and t_2min cells light up green and amber.
on_screen_text: Illustration in SQL, not Spark itself
Only 2 min 40 s behind in event time
scenes.narration: Let's run the rule on our table as plain SQL. This illustrates the arithmetic; it is not Spark's engine. Go through events in arrival order and track the max event time seen so far. When event 6 finally arrives at 09:21:40, the latest event time seen is 09:06:40, from event 8. Event 6 happened at 09:04. So it's only two minutes forty seconds behind in event time. With a ten-minute threshold, it's inside: guaranteed. With a two-minute threshold, it's outside: best effort.

steps.label: Event 6: only 2 min 40 s behind max event time

scenes.beat: Comparison: left '17 min 40 s delay (wall clock)', right '2 min 40 s behind (event time)'; the right one gets the tick.
on_screen_text: Lateness is measured in event time
Watermark moves only with newer events
scenes.narration: That's the trap. Event 6 was delayed seventeen minutes on the wall clock, but the watermark is built from event times. Nothing newer than 09:06:40 had arrived, so the watermark was still 09:06:40 minus the threshold. What counts is how far behind the latest event time a row is, not how long it spent in transit.

props.verdict: Watermark moves only with newer events

scenes.beat: Callout takeaway card.
on_screen_text: Takeaway: watermark = max event time - threshold
scenes.narration: Takeaway: watermark equals max event time minus threshold. Inside it, guaranteed. Outside it, best effort.

scenes.beat: Hook card; a 'run' button is pressed twice and the output counter stays the same.
scenes.narration: Assume your pipeline runs twice. Retries make it likely. Make twice look exactly like once.

scenes.beat: RowHighlight on the events table: both copies of event 3 glow, with '44 s apart' between them.
scenes.narration: Idempotent means running a step twice gives the same result as running it once. You need it because retries are normal: a network blip, a producer resend, a job replayed from its last checkpoint. Our table already shows it. Event 3, the click by user 102, arrived twice, 44 seconds apart.

scenes.beat: FlowGraph: producer sends message seq 7, times out, resends seq 7; the broker box stamps the second copy 'duplicate' and keeps one.
on_screen_text: Broker spots the resend and dedupes it
scenes.narration: Kafka handles one source of duplicates for you. With the idempotent producer, each producer has an ID and every message it sends carries a sequence number. If it resends after a timeout, the broker recognises the same producer ID and sequence number and dedupes it. But that only covers producer retries into Kafka. Duplicates can still come from elsewhere, so the sink has to defend itself too.

scenes.beat: CodePanel with the CREATE TABLE and both INSERTs; a row counter runs 0 -> 8 on the first load and stays at 8 on the retry.
on_screen_text: Load 9 rows, then retry the load
scenes.narration: In DuckDB, the cleanest guard is an enforced key. Give the table a primary key on event_id and insert with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. In DuckDB, ON CONFLICT needs a primary key or unique constraint to check against. We load all nine raw rows, then run the exact same load again, like a retried job. The duplicate copy of event 3 is skipped the first time, and the whole retry is skipped the second time. Eight rows, eight unique events. Run it a third time and nothing changes. That's idempotent.

scenes.beat: FlowGraph: source box labelled 'replayable' and sink box labelled 'idempotent' light up; a replay arrow loops back without changing the sink's row count.
scenes.narration: Spark's docs describe how Structured Streaming can ensure end-to-end exactly-once: replayable sources, tracked with offsets and checkpoints, plus idempotent sinks. The source lets you redo work after a failure. The sink makes redoing it harmless. In Spark, it's those two properties together.

scenes.beat: CodePanel shows withWatermark("event_time", ...).dropDuplicates("event_id", "event_time") next to a watermark line.
on_screen_text: With watermark: key on event_id + event_time
scenes.narration: You can also dedupe inside the stream. With a watermark, Spark dedupes on event_id plus event time, or with dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark on event_id.

props.text: With a watermark: dropDuplicates on event_id + event_time
props.label: Spark

scenes.beat: Callout takeaway card.
on_screen_text: Takeaway: assume every step runs twice
Key on event_id. Make the sink idempotent.
scenes.narration: Takeaway: assume every step runs twice. Key on event_id, and make the sink idempotent.

props.label: Takeaway
props.detail: Key on event_id. Make the sink idempotent.

scenes.beat: Hook card; a dashboard tile shows 4, which flips to 3.
scenes.narration: Your dashboard says four clicks. There were three. Here's the layering that fixes it.

scenes.beat: FlowGraph: three stacked layers, bronze, silver, gold, fill in from left to right.
on_screen_text: Bronze: raw, unvalidated, as it arrived
Gold: aggregated for dashboards and BI
scenes.narration: The medallion architecture, as Databricks describes it, has three layers. Bronze holds raw, unvalidated data, as it arrived. Silver is cleaned, validated and deduplicated. Gold is aggregated, business-level data for analytics and reporting. Our nine-row events table, duplicate and all, is bronze.

scenes.beat: CodePanel + DataTable; the click count of 4 is circled and both event 3 rows are traced back to it.
scenes.narration: Count straight from bronze and you get four clicks. The retry of event 3 is counted twice. That's the four from the hook.

scenes.beat: CodePanel; the two event 3 rows get rn 1 and 2; rn 2 fades out and the table shrinks to 8 rows.
scenes.narration: Silver removes the duplicate. ROW_NUMBER, partitioned by event_id and ordered by ingest_time, numbers every copy of an event. Keep row number one, the first arrival, and drop the rest. Nine rows in, eight out. Unlike ON CONFLICT, this is just a query, so it needs no constraint, and you can rerun it from bronze whenever your cleaning rules change.

steps.label: Number each copy of an event

scenes.beat: CodePanel; silver rows collapse into three gold rows; the click tile on the dashboard updates to 3.
scenes.narration: Gold is what the dashboard reads. Group silver by event date and event type, and count events and distinct users. Three clicks, three page views, two purchases. Now the dashboard says three, because it reads from deduplicated silver, not raw bronze.

props.title: gold: events per day and type

scenes.beat: FlowGraph: a 'fix dedupe rule' patch is applied to the silver step; silver and gold rebuild from the untouched bronze layer.
on_screen_text: Rules change: rebuild silver from raw
scenes.narration: Why keep bronze at all? Because cleaning rules change. If you find a bug in your dedupe, you fix the query and rebuild silver from bronze. If you had cleaned on the way in, the raw events would be gone.

scenes.beat: Callout takeaway card.
scenes.narration: Takeaway: bronze keeps, silver fixes, gold answers.

props.text: Bronze keeps, silver fixes, gold answers.
props.label: Takeaway

scenes.beat: Hook card; a grid of date partitions where only one tile lights up.
on_screen_text: Pruning needs a filter on the partition column.
Miss it, and no partition is skipped.
scenes.narration: Partition pruning only kicks in when your query filters on the partition column.

props.title: Pruning needs a filter on the partition column.
props.subtitle: Miss it, and no partition is skipped.

scenes.beat: PartitionGrid: a month of date tiles; rows drop into the tile for their event_date.
on_screen_text: Each day stored in its own partition
scenes.narration: Our silver table grows every day, so we partition it by event_date: each day's rows are stored in their own partition. In BigQuery that's a partitioned table. In a data lake it's often Hive-style folders, one per value, like event_date equals 2026-10-19.

scenes.beat: CodePanel with the query; on the PartitionGrid every tile except 2026-10-19 greys out; a 'bytes scanned' bar shrinks.
on_screen_text: Filter on partition column: skip the rest
DuckDB: filter pushed into Hive partitions
scenes.narration: Now a query that filters on the partition column. BigQuery's docs call this pruning: with a qualifying filter on the partitioning column, it scans only the matching partitions and skips the rest, which reduces the bytes processed. DuckDB does the same with Hive-partitioned files: filters on the partition keys are pushed down, so non-matching partitions are skipped. Here we run the query on an in-memory table, so the result is real, but the skipping only happens on partitioned storage.

scenes.beat: Comparison: left 'WHERE user_id = 101' lights up every tile; right 'WHERE event_date = ...' lights up one.
on_screen_text: Filter only on user_id? No partition skipped
The filter must hit the partition column
Partition by what you filter by
scenes.narration: The trap: filter only on user_id and there's no qualifying filter on event_date, so every day's partition still has to be read. Partitioning helps the queries that filter on the partition column. So pick that column from how the table is actually queried. For our dashboard, that's the date.

props.verdict: Partition by what you filter by

scenes.beat: Callout takeaway card.
on_screen_text: Takeaway: partition by what you filter by
scenes.narration: Takeaway: partition by what you filter by.

props.text: Partition by what you filter by
props.label: Takeaway

scenes.beat: ListCard: the six chapter cards stack while the click dot from the cold open retraces the full pipeline from Kafka to the dashboard tile.
on_screen_text: Kafka: key by user_id, order per partition
scenes.narration: Let's recap the whole pipeline. Clicks go into Kafka, keyed by user_id, so each user's events stay ordered within a partition. Whether you run batch or streaming, you count by event time. Late events are handled by a watermark: max event time seen minus a threshold, guaranteed inside, best effort outside. Every write is idempotent: a replayable source plus a sink keyed on event_id. Data flows bronze to silver to gold. And silver is partitioned by event_date, so queries filtering on date skip the other days.

events.label: Kafka: key by user_id, order per partition

scenes.beat: EndCard with the website and tagline; watermark queryunstuck.
scenes.narration: That's the clickstream pipeline, end to end, on nine rows. If this helped, you'll find more visual explanations like it at queryunstuck.in.

code_blocks.code:
SELECT event_id, user_id, event_type,
       strftime(event_time, '%H:%M:%S')  AS event_at,
       strftime(ingest_time, '%H:%M:%S') AS arrived_at
FROM events
ORDER BY ingest_time;

SELECT event_id, event_type,
       strftime(event_time, '%H:%M:%S')  AS event_at,
       strftime(ingest_time, '%H:%M:%S') AS arrived_at,
       ingest_time - event_time          AS lag
FROM events
ORDER BY ingest_time;

-- Illustration of the watermark rule, not Spark itself
WITH seen AS (
  SELECT *, MAX(event_time) OVER (ORDER BY ingest_time) AS max_seen
  FROM events
)
SELECT event_id,
       strftime(event_time, '%H:%M:%S') AS event_at,
       strftime(max_seen, '%H:%M:%S')   AS max_seen_at,
       max_seen - event_time            AS behind,
       CASE WHEN max_seen - event_time < INTERVAL 10 MINUTE
            THEN 'guaranteed' ELSE 'best effort' END AS t_10min,
       CASE WHEN max_seen - event_time < INTERVAL 2 MINUTE
            THEN 'guaranteed' ELSE 'best effort' END AS t_2min
FROM seen
ORDER BY ingest_time;
